title: How Beautiful the Feet: Your God Reigns
summary: Zion is told to wake, put on her beautiful garments, and shake off the dust and chains of captivity, because the LORD will redeem her without money. A messenger runs across the mountains with good news, the watchmen shout for joy, and the exiles are told to leave Babylon, carrying the temple vessels, with God going before and behind them. The chapter ends by introducing the Servant who will be highly exalted after being disfigured beyond human likeness, the opening of the fourth Servant Song.
story: The double call “Awake, awake” that began in 51:9 and 51:17 reaches its third and final form here, addressed to Zion herself. Everything in chapters 40 to 51 has been building toward this: the announcement that God is coming home to Jerusalem and bringing his people with him. Verses 7 to 12 are the high point of that announcement. Then, with no transition, verse 13 begins the fourth and last Servant Song, which runs to the end of chapter 53. The placement matters. The good news of God's reign and the suffering of the Servant sit side by side, and the song explains how God's victory will actually be won.
historical: Verses 4 and 5 compress Israel's history of oppression into three stages: Egypt, where Jacob's family went down to live and later became slaves; Assyria, which destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC and devastated Judah in 701 BC; and now a third power, unnamed but clearly Babylon, which had taken Judah captive. The command to leave “from there” (verse 11) fits the moment after Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC and permitted exiled peoples to return home. Ezra 1:7-11 records that Cyrus gave back the gold and silver temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried off, and that they were brought to Jerusalem by those who returned. This chapter's instruction to those who carry the vessels to purify themselves fits that event closely, whether read as contemporary address or as prophecy of it.
cultural:
News in the ancient world traveled on foot. A runner coming over the hills toward a city could be seen by the watchmen on its walls long before he arrived, and they read his news from his pace and bearing (compare 2 Samuel 18:24-27, where David's watchman recognizes a runner by the way he runs). The messenger of verse 7 brings the best possible news: peace, salvation, and the words “Your God reigns.” To a people whose God had seemed defeated by Babylon's gods, this was the announcement that he was king after all.

The instructions for departure deliberately recall the exodus while changing it. At the first Passover Israel ate in haste, ready to flee Egypt (Exodus 12:11). This time, verse 12 says, they will not leave in a hurry, because the LORD goes before them and guards the rear, as the pillar of cloud once did (Exodus 14:19-20). The call to touch nothing unclean reflects the priestly holiness required of those who carried the sacred vessels (Numbers 4:15).
literary: The chapter has three movements. Verses 1 to 6 are God's call to Zion and an explanation of why he must act: his people are taken for nothing and his name is blasphemed. Verses 7 to 12 are a scene: the runner, the watchmen, the ruins breaking into song, and the command to depart. Verses 13 to 15 begin the fourth Servant Song, which scholars usually treat as a unit running from 52:13 to 53:12. The chapter break before 53:1, added in the Middle Ages, separates the song's first stanza from the rest. The song opens and closes with God speaking about his Servant, and its first stanza states the whole paradox in advance: the Servant will be raised high, yet many were appalled at his disfigurement, and kings will fall silent before something they have never been told.

outline.t: Zion, wake and put on your beautiful garments
Sold for nothing, redeemed without money
The messenger on the mountains: your God reigns
Depart, depart: the LORD goes before and behind
The fourth Servant Song begins: exalted and disfigured

doctrines.note: “Your God reigns” (verse 7) is the heart of the good news here. The return from exile is not only relief for Israel but a public demonstration that the LORD is king over the nations, before the eyes of all the ends of the earth.
Those who carry the LORD's vessels must purify themselves and touch no unclean thing. The redeemed people are called out of Babylon's world, not only its territory, to belong to a holy God.

The Servant introduced in verses 13 to 15 will be exalted after terrible suffering and will affect many nations and kings. The chapter holds these together without yet explaining how; chapter 53 does.

words.note: Basar, to bring news, especially good news. The one who brings it (verse 7) is the mevasser, the herald. When Greek-speaking Jews translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek (the Septuagint, in the last centuries BC), they used the verb from which the New Testament's word for gospel comes. The gospel in the New Testament is this announcement: God reigns.

Sakal, to act wisely, and so to succeed. The BSB translates “My Servant will prosper” (verse 13); other translations have “act wisely.” The word joins skill and success: the Servant's path will turn out to have been the wise one, however it looks at the time.

Nazah, to spatter or sprinkle, the verb used for priests sprinkling blood or water in purification rites (Leviticus 4:6; 16:14). “So He will sprinkle many nations” (verse 15) suggests a priestly act of cleansing. The Septuagint instead reads that many nations will marvel at him, and some modern translations follow that sense. Both readings fit the verse's contrast between horror and awe.

christ: Paul quotes verse 7 in Romans 10:15 to describe those sent to preach Christ, and the New Testament's word for the gospel comes from the language of this messenger who announces God's reign. Jesus began his preaching with the same news, that the kingdom of God had come near (Mark 1:14-15). Paul also quotes verse 5 in Romans 2:24, verse 11 in 2 Corinthians 6:17, and verse 15 in Romans 15:21, where he explains his mission to preach where Christ had not been named. Most striking is the join between verse 12 and verse 13. The announcement that God reigns is followed at once by a Servant who is disfigured and then exalted. The New Testament reads Jesus's crucifixion and resurrection as exactly that pattern: the way God's reign actually arrives.
questions: Why do you think the announcement “Your God reigns” is followed immediately by the portrait of a suffering Servant?
Verse 12 promises that God goes before and behind his people. Where do you most need to know that he guards the rear, the past you are leaving?
The watchmen shout because they see the LORD returning to Zion. What would it look like to be a watchman for good news in your community?
